chunks: Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Abi Najran, from 'Asim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abi Ja'far عليه السلام, who said:

Amir al-Mu'minin عليه السلام gave judgment regarding a man who had snatched a garment from the market. They said, "This man has stolen." So he said: "Indeed, I do not amputate for open, brazen snatching; rather, I amputate the hand of one who takes and then conceals."

key_terms.أَقْطَعُ: I inflict amputation as the legal hadd punishment
key_terms.اخْتَلَسَ: snatched or took swiftly in an open manner
key_terms.الزَّعَارَّةِ الْمُعْلَنَةِ: open and brazen public snatching, not treated here as hadd-level theft
key_terms.السُّوقِ: the marketplace where the incident occurred
key_terms.ثَوْبًا: a garment that was the object taken
key_terms.سَرَقَ: stole; unlawfully took property in the sense under discussion
key_terms.يُخْفِي: conceals the taken property, indicating clandestine theft

ai.seo_question: Does the hadd of theft apply to openly snatching an item from the market?
ai.summary: This hadith records a legal ruling from Amir al-Mu'minin عليه السلام distinguishing between openly snatching property and theft that is taken and concealed. It shows that the hadd punishment for theft is not applied to every form of unlawful taking, but depends on the specific legal definition of sariqah.
